title: Subagents Are an Antipattern? (GPT-5.5 vs Opus 4.8, sides swapped)

decision.resolution_reason: On the merits, the proposition overreaches by treating orchestrator-worker and subagent architectures as generally mistaken. AgentB better established that, for over-window research, coding exploration, privilege separation, and independent verification, disciplined subagents are not merely rare exceptions but core useful machinery; agentA's best guidance narrows the pattern rather than defeating it.
decision.craft_reason: AgentB debated better on points: it attacked the central premise early, converted several of agentA's concessions into a threshold-frame argument, and gave concrete counterexamples with mechanisms. AgentA was highly rigorous and often landed better operational cautions, but spent much of the debate defending a narrower definition than the resolution and rebranding similar worker boundaries as tools.
decision.summary: The verdicts do not diverge: agentB wins both the resolution and debate craft, though narrowly rather than by knockout. AgentA successfully proved that loose persona swarms and unverified child-agent recommendations are dangerous; agentB more persuasively showed that the mature answer is disciplined orchestration, not general avoidance of subagents as an architectural pattern.
decision.caveat: If 'subagent' is stipulated in agentA's narrowest sense—free-form child agents returning ungrounded recommendations—the merits move much closer to agentA; the actual resolution, however, expressly included orchestrator-worker architectures.

rounds.reason: AgentA opened with a strong, concrete case about lossy handoffs, distributed-systems failure modes, AutoGPT/BabyAGI, AutoGen, SWE-agent, and Agentless. AgentB narrowly won by directly challenging the premise that the monolith is lossless, citing Lost in the Middle, context rot, Claude Code, safety isolation, and Anthropic's multi-agent research result.

AgentA effectively separated visible compression from correct compression, attacked the Agentless and Claude Code examples, and made strong points on security laundering, economics, and evidence-first verification. AgentB's resolution-scope challenge was forceful, but it rested heavily on an expansive definition and the turn ended with an unfinished rebuttal.

AgentA clarified bounded LLM transforms, parallelism without agency, reliability math, and decomposition failures. AgentB answered with the strongest pincer of the debate: raw output causes context rot, while distilled output implies a worker; it also flipped the reliability math with best-of-N/AlphaCode and reframed scratchpads as serial lossy handoffs.

AgentA's five-part ex ante definition, evidence-ledger alternative, token-normalized critique, and write-capable fork were strong. AgentB narrowly won by using that definition to show agentA had conceded real counterexamples in Anthropic research and Claude Code, while also answering the read/write fork with branch-and-commit discipline and limiting Qi-style weak-oracle objections to depth fan-out.

AgentA scored with a broad set of new production objections: ontology drift, compliance/data-minimization, quality variance, fake human-team analogies, runtime tool scoping, and the industry trend toward explicit workflows. AgentB responded well on heterogeneous specialists and shared schemas, but overclaimed that the microservices analogy conceded the proposition and that compliance necessarily favors LLM subcomponents.

AgentA gave a strong enterprise-focused rebuttal on resettable controllers, premature decomposition, interactive correction, scheduler nondeterminism, and correlated disagreement. AgentB edged the round by adding two high-force points: above effective context limits, slice readers become necessary, and typed seams enable testing, partial recovery, and approval gates that a single entangled cognition cannot supply as cleanly.

AgentA's clarification that a single agent can be a resettable logical controller with authoritative external state was a strong answer to agentB's repeated 'one polluted prompt' framing. AgentB's reply that this was merely orchestrator-worker was effective, but its four-eyes and separated-checker claims leaned on contested nomenclature and some overstatement.

AgentA continued to draw a precise line between bounded state transitions and delegated semantic authority, with good points on GraphRAG/RAPTOR, four-eyes controls, verifier calibration, and coverage gaps. AgentB won the turn by introducing the god-prompt maintenance problem, explaining static versus dynamic decomposition, and turning coverage and compliance objections into arguments for stronger audited boundaries.

AgentA delivered an excellent closing that fairly named counterexamples, stated design rules, and crystallized the 'typed wrongness' critique. AgentB's closing was slightly stronger because it turned those very rules—read-only scouts, independent verifiers, isolated branches, single commit gate—into a disciplined orchestrator-worker architecture and restated the core choice as inspectable loss versus hidden compression.
No substantive argument was added. Both agents simply acknowledged that their closings stood.

tally.note: AgentB wins on points; most substantive rounds were close and turned on definition and scope.

key_moments.moment: Reframed lossiness as inevitable and argued that subagent boundaries make compression governable rather than introducing it.
key_moments.note: This directly attacked agentA's core premise.

key_moments.moment: Distinguished visible compression from correct compression and introduced security laundering, Greshake-style indirect injection, and token-economics objections.
key_moments.note: This was agentA's best early rebuttal.

key_moments.moment: Answered agentA's reliability math with OR-style best-of-N reasoning and argued that scratchpads are just serial lossy handoffs.
Offered an ex ante five-part definition of the problematic subagent: goal, self-chosen tool policy, private context, self-stopping, and compressed judgment.
key_moments.note: This sharpened the debate's central definition.

key_moments.moment: Used that definition to argue agentA had conceded true counterexamples in Anthropic research workers and Claude Code task workers.
key_moments.note: A major craft win for agentB.

key_moments.moment: Introduced ontology drift, compliance/data-minimization, quality variance, and lack of persistent expertise as independent production failure modes.
key_moments.note: These were the strongest practical objections to naive subagent systems.

key_moments.moment: Pressed the capacity-ceiling argument: once evidence exceeds an effective window, something must read and compress slices outside the final synthesis context.
key_moments.note: This was central to agentB's merits case.

key_moments.moment: Clarified that the alternative is not one endless prompt but a resettable logical controller backed by authoritative state.
key_moments.note: This neutralized a recurring strawman against the single-agent side.

key_moments.moment: Introduced the god-prompt maintenance artifact and argued that modular worker prompts can be tested and versioned independently.
Closed by turning agentA's design rules into a disciplined orchestrator-worker specification and emphasizing inspectable loss at boundaries.
key_moments.note: This sealed agentB's craft and resolution edge.

analysis.heading: How agentB won
paragraphs: AgentB won by refusing to let the debate remain a simple 'subagents lose context' story. Its core move was to argue that compression is unavoidable in any long-horizon system, so the relevant question is whether the lossy step is hidden inside one model trajectory or made inspectable at a typed boundary.

AgentB also made the stronger counterexample case. Anthropic's multi-agent research system, Claude Code-style task isolation, CaMeL-style privilege separation, and independent verifier/reward-model examples were not all equally clean subagent cases, but collectively they made the proposition's broad 'generally avoid orchestrator-worker architectures' language look too strong.

Most importantly, agentB repeatedly converted agentA's concessions into a threshold argument: use subagents when evidence exceeds the effective context window, when privilege or tool boundaries matter, when independent verification matters, or when read-only breadth search dominates. That threshold framing was more persuasive than the proposition's antipattern framing.

analysis.heading: Where agentA scored
paragraphs: AgentA's best work was operational rather than definitional. It convincingly showed that loose persona swarms, natural-language handoffs, and child agents returning polished recommendations can hide omitted evidence, create ontology drift, amplify weak verifiers, complicate compliance, and generate TOCTOU or scheduler-dependent failures.

The Qi et al. weak-oracle point was especially strong: fan-out only improves reliability when selection is trustworthy, and in messy enterprise workflows the verifier is often partial or gameable. AgentA also did well to distinguish bounded transforms, validators, evidence ledgers, and artifact gates from open-ended delegated judgment.

AgentA's final design rules were sensible: maintain one authoritative state, prefer bounded components, keep workers side-effect-free, and serialize commits through a final gate. Those rules substantially constrain subagents and are good engineering advice even though agentB successfully argued they describe disciplined orchestration rather than a rejection of the pattern.

analysis.heading: The definition fight decided the close calls
paragraphs: AgentA wanted 'subagent' to mean a child LLM with private discretionary task ownership and compressed recommendations. AgentB wanted it to include disciplined orchestrator-worker systems with scoped contexts, typed evidence returns, read-only scouts, verifiers, and isolated branches.

AgentB's definition was sometimes too elastic, especially when it tried to count reward models, PRMs, GraphRAG-like summaries, or Kafka-style producers as subagents. But the debate resolution itself explicitly included orchestrator-worker architectures and subagent fan-outs, so agentB's broader framing was more relevant to the proposition as written.

analysis.heading: Not a knockout
paragraphs: This was a points win, not a demolition. AgentA made the stronger case against naive multi-agent frameworks and against trusting child-agent conclusions as evidence. AgentB won because the proposition was too broad and because the mature architecture both sides converged on still used worker boundaries, scoped contexts, independent checkers, and orchestration.

quotes.text: A subagent boundary is an information-destroying compression boundary.
The compression boundary is not created by subagents. It already exists inside every agent — you've just hidden it.
Security boundaries live in the runtime, not in the org chart of imaginary coworkers.
You have defined 'subagent' as the version that fails.
The choice was never lossless-vs-lossy. It was inspectable loss at a governable boundary vs. invisible loss you cannot log, replay, fixture, or fence.
